about: FORTY RARE EVENTS (Design/fate_faith_and_self.md section 5): things seen once in a life, or once in the game. Written 7 Oct 2026. Each has a true date, to the day where the records give one, or a once-a-life chance; where it can be met; what is seen in the ship window and what the log says; one card of two or three choices in the engine's card format (stage, when, once, options with key, label, check, cost and effects: Code/Core/Encounters/EncounterDef.cs, Effects.cs); and its source. 'life': first (it can be met in 793 to about 806, on or near the twelve ports of the first release), later (it belongs to a later life or to water outside the twelve), word (it comes only as news in the first release). 'fire' is the day the game shows a dated one (the engine's conditions know year and month, not the day: a dated card is put on the scheduler for its day). Dates are Julian. THE SKY WAS CHECKED against the NASA Five Millennium catalogs of solar and lunar eclipses (Espenak and Meeus; read 7 Oct 2026; times are Terrestrial Time, about three quarters of an hour ahead of clock time in 800) and against the annals: 'recorded' true means an annal of the time has it; false means it is reckoned only, and the game may show it but no chronicle line names it. No eclipse of the sun could be seen from the North Sea between 793 and 805: do not invent one. RULES: rare means rare: at most once each; a chance of 0.3 means three lives in ten meet it. A player should end a life having met five or six. Signs are read, never proved: a card never says what a sign meant, and where it offers readings, each is one crewman's or one faith's. Stat changes the engine has no verb for are under 'stats' (see self_793.json). (?) marks what was not checked; LATER a source written long after. A draft for the user to overwrite.

rules.expected_in_a_life: Of the 24 that can be met in the first life, 13 are dated and need the right port in the right month; 11 are by chance, at 0.2 to 0.4 a life. That gives about three by chance and two or three by date.
rules.moon_card: The four darkened moons of the first life share one card (rare.moon_dark), shown at most twice in a life.

where.when: year = 793 and month >= 5 and month <= 7 and port.realm = franks

seen.window: Corn standing thick and pale along the bank, in a year when there is none.
seen.log: Corn in the fields, in the hungry year. The men who went ashore say the ears are empty.

card.when: year = 793 and month >= 5 and month <= 7
card.title: Corn that is not corn
card.intention: The bank is yellow with grain. Nobody is reaping it.

options.label: Send a man ashore to cut a sheaf
Ask the oldest hand aboard what it is
Keep to the stream

events.source: Annales Mosellani 792 (=793): false grain in fields, woods and marshes that could be seen and touched but not eaten; Synod of Frankfurt 794 c. 25 (MGH Capit. I no. 28): in the year of the great hunger 'empty corn' was seen, 'eaten by demons', and voices of reproach heard

events.date: 793, before 8 June; no day is given

where.water: north of the Humber, outside the twelve

seen.window: Nothing, in the first release: it is told with the news of the holy island. If the game begins on 1 May, once at night in May, low in the north, a red light that moves.
seen.log: They say that before it happened there were sheets of light over Northumbria, and whirlwinds, and fiery dragons flying in the air.

card.when: year = 793 and month >= 6
card.title: What the sky said
card.intention: The crew has heard about the dragons. Each man knows what they meant.

options.label: Go by the Christian reading: a warning, for sins
Go by the old one: a drake flies where gold is about to change hands
Say it was weather, and set the watch

events.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (D, E) 793; Alcuin, letter 16 (in Lent a rain of blood fell from a clear sky on the north side of Saint Peter's at York); Beowulf 2270-2280 for the drake that guards gold

events.date: 796-03-28, between cock-crow and dawn (the Monday of Holy Week)
events.nasa: total; greatest eclipse 06:49 TT on 28 March, so the moon set darkened over England and the Channel

also_reckoned.what: total, in the evening (greatest 20:23 TT): seen everywhere, written down by no one we have
total, about midnight of 2 to 3 November (00:08 TT)

seen.window: The moon going down the western sky with a bite out of it, then the colour of old copper.
seen.log: The moon was darkened between cock-crow and dawn.

card.when: (year = 796 and (month = 3 or month = 9)) or (year = 800 and month = 1) or (year = 802 and month = 5) or (year = 803 and month = 11)
card.title: Win, moon!
card.intention: The watch is beating on the gunwale and shouting at the sky. It is an old thing: you shout to help her.

options.label: Let them shout
Forbid it: the priests call it heathen
Tell them what the books say: it is the earth's own shadow

shout.troth: -1 if me.faith = christian; +1 if me.faith = old_gods

events.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (D, E) 795 (=796): 'v Kal. Apr.'; Historia regum 796; NASA lunar catalog. Three weeks later, on 18 April, king Aethelred of Northumbria was killed, and men put the two together. The shouting: Indiculus superstitionum, head 21. The shadow: Bede, De natura rerum c. 22

where.when: ((year = 797 and month >= 8) or (year = 798 and month <= 7)) and moored

seen.window: Nothing: that is the point.
seen.log: A clerk asked whether we had seen the red star at sea this year. Nobody has.

card.when: ((year = 797 and month >= 8) or (year = 798 and month <= 7)) and moored and (port.id = traiectum or port.id = quentovic)
card.title: The star that is not there
card.intention: A clerk with ink on his sleeve is asking every skipper the same question: when did you last see the red star?

options.label: Tell him: not since last summer
Ask him what it means when a star goes missing
Say you steer by the other ones

events.source: ARF 798: the star called Mars could not be seen anywhere in the whole sky from July of the year before to July of this year

events.date: 800-01-15, in the evening; and 802-05-21, before dawn
events.nasa: 15 January 800: partial, greatest 21:29 TT. 21 May 802: total, greatest 05:01 TT.

seen.window: January: a bitten moon over the frozen hard, in the winter port. May: a red moon going down into the sea before sunrise.
seen.log: The moon was darkened.

events.correction: The Chronicle puts the first 'at the second hour of the night on xvii Kal. Feb.', which is 16 January: the night is counted to the day that follows, and the eclipse was on the evening of the 15th. It puts the second 'at dawn on xiii Kal. Ian.', 20 December 802, when there was no eclipse: almost surely a slip for xiii Kal. Iun., 20 May, the night before the total eclipse of 21 May. chronicle_793.json has these as 800-01-16-lunar-eclipse and 802-12-20-lunar-eclipse (the second already marked doubtful): move the second to 802-05-21.
events.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (A) 800, 802; NASA lunar catalog

where.when: year = 800 and month = 7 and port.realm = franks

seen.window: White on the thwarts and the mooring ropes at dawn, in July.
seen.log: A hard frost this morning, the day before the Nones of July. The corn is in ear.

card.when: year = 800 and month = 7 and moored and port.realm = franks
card.title: Frost in July
card.intention: The quay is talking of nothing else. Half of it is buying grain.

options.label: Buy grain now, before the harvest fails
Wait and see the fields for yourself
Sell what grain you have, at today's fright

events.then: The annal says the frost did no harm to the crops. Grain bought in the fright is worth less in a month: the card does not say so.
events.source: ARF 800: an unusual hard frost on 6 July and again on 9 July, which did the crops no harm

events.date: 801-04-30 in Italy, at the second hour of the night; the Rhine lands the same year, no day; again round Aachen in the winter of 803

where.when: year = 801 and month >= 5 and moored and port.realm = franks

seen.window: The river shivers flat, with no wind. A bell rings once with nobody at the rope.
seen.log: The ground shook. The church bell rang by itself.

card.when: year = 801 and month >= 5 and moored and (port.id = dorestad or port.id = traiectum or port.id = daventre)
card.title: The ground moves
card.intention: It lasts as long as a Pater noster. A storehouse wall has come down on the bank.

options.label: Put the crew to digging out the neighbour's store
Get the boat off the bank and into the stream
Go up to the church with everyone else

events.source: ARF 801 (a great earthquake in Italy on 30 April: the roof of Saint Paul's at Rome fell; the same year places by the Rhine, in Gaul and in Germany shook; a sickness followed the mild winter); ARF 803 (an earthquake round the palace at Aachen, and a dying after it)

events.date: 806-06-04 at dawn (a cross in the moon); 806-08-30 (a ring round the sun); 806-09-01 at night (the moon darkened)
events.nasa: 1 September 806: total eclipse of the moon, greatest 23:26 TT. The Frankish annals put it on 2 September (the night counted forward).

seen.window: June: a pale cross through the setting moon. August: a ring wide as a hand at arm's length round the sun. September: the moon red at midnight.
seen.log: A cross was seen in the moon at dawn.

card.when: year = 806 and month >= 6 and month <= 9
card.title: Three in one summer
card.intention: A cross in the moon, a ring round the sun, and now the moon gone dark. The crew wants to be told something.

options.label: Say what the old hands say: a reign is ending somewhere
Say what a seaman knows: a ring round the sun means wind in two days
Say nothing, and stand the watch yourself

events.then: That year the king of the Northumbrians was driven from his kingdom and sixty-eight of the brothers of Hi were killed. The card does not say so.
events.doubt: The Chronicle is said to call 4 June a Wednesday; by the reckoning in calendar_793.json it was a Thursday (?).
events.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (D, E) 806; ARF 807; NASA lunar catalog

events.date: 807-01-31 (the star Jupiter seemed to pass through the moon); 807-02-11 at noon (the sun darkened); 807-02-26 (the moon darkened, and battle lines seen in the sky that night); 807-03-17 and eight days after (a small dark spot on the sun); 807-08-22 (the moon darkened at the third hour of the night)
events.nasa: moon: 26 February 807 total (03:43 TT); 21 August 807 partial (23:40 TT). The eclipse of the sun on 11 February was not checked against the catalog (?).

seen.window: A year in which the sky will not keep still.
seen.log: The sun was darkened at noon.

card.when: year = 807 and month >= 2 and month <= 3
card.title: The spot on the sun
card.intention: Through the haze at sunrise there is a black speck on the sun. It was there yesterday.

options.label: Have the boy mark each day it stays
Tell them not to stare at the sun

events.source: ARF 807, the fullest sky record of the age (the spot, which the annalist took for the star Mercury, is a sunspot)

events.date: 809-07-16, a Monday, at the start of the fifth hour of the day (England); 810-11-30 (Francia)
events.nasa: 30 November 810: total, greatest over the lower Danube (46 N, 27 E): a deep partial eclipse on the Rhine. Moon: 20 June 810 total (20:38 TT); 14 December 810 total (18:54 TT).

seen.window: The light goes thin and cold in the middle of the day; shadows have two edges.
seen.log: The sun was darkened.

card.when: (year = 809 and month = 7) or (year = 810 and month = 11) or (year = 840 and month = 5) or (year = 1030 and month = 8)
card.title: Noon goes out
card.intention: The gulls have stopped. The steersman has let go of the helm to look.

options.label: Take the helm yourself and hold the course
Let each man call on what he calls on
Put about for the nearest landing

events.correction: The fate page has 'two darkenings of the sun in 810'. The annals list two (7 June and 30 November) and two of the moon (21 June and 15 December). The June one could not be seen from Francia and was most likely reckoned, not seen (?); the November one was real. The eclipse of 16 July 809 is the English one.
events.source: ARF 810; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 809; NASA solar and lunar catalogs

events.date: seen in Francia in Easter week 837 (Easter was 1 April); nearest the earth on 10 to 11 April; in the Chinese record from 22 March

seen.window: A star with a tail a third of the sky long, moving a hand's breadth a night.
seen.log: A star with hair, in the sign of the Virgin. It moves.

card.when: (year = 837 and month = 4) or (year = 912 and month = 7) or (year = 989 and month >= 8 and month <= 9) or (year = 1066 and month >= 4 and month <= 5)
card.title: The long-haired star
card.intention: Nobody aboard has seen one. Everybody aboard knows what it means: a great man's death, a change in the realm.

options.label: Ask each man whose death he thinks it is
Give alms at the next church, as the emperor did
Note where it stands and steer by it while it lasts

events.source: The Astronomer, Vita Hludowici c. 58 (the emperor asks him what it means, orders alms and prayers, and then goes hunting); the comet is Halley's: perihelion 28 February 837 and the nearest pass ever, about 0.03 of the earth's distance from the sun (Yeomans and Kiang 1981 (?)). The same summer Walichrum was raided and its count killed.

events.date: 840-05-05, a Wednesday, the eve of the Ascension
events.nasa: total; greatest at 43 N, 11 W, the track running across Gaul to the Alps

seen.window: Full night at mid-afternoon, and stars.
seen.log: The sun was darkened on the eve of the Ascension, so that the stars were seen.

events.then: The old emperor Louis died on 20 June, forty-six days later, on an island in the Rhine.
events.source: The Astronomer, Vita Hludowici c. 62; Annales Bertiniani 840; Annales Fuldenses 840; NASA solar catalog

seen.window: A hairy star low in the north-west after sunset.
seen.log: A dark and rainy year. A star with hair appeared.

events.source: Annals of Ulster 912 ('a dark and rainy year; a comet appeared'); it is Halley's (en.wikipedia.org 'Halley's Comet', read 7 Oct 2026)

events.date: 939, for a day and a half; dim suns and hard winters to 942

seen.window: A sun the colour of blood that can be looked at, and a sky like dirty wool.
seen.log: The sun was the colour of blood from the start of one day to the middle of the next.

card.when: year = 939 and month >= 5 and month <= 9
card.title: The red sun
card.intention: It has no heat in it. The barley on the shore is a hand high and yellow.

options.label: Buy grain and salt fish now, at any price
Take her south for the year
Trade as in any year

events.then: Here the sign is true: the hungry years come. It is the one card of this kind that pays the careful.
events.source: Chronicon Scotorum under 939; Annales Casinates; the eruption of Eldgja in Iceland, begun 939 and ended 940 or later, with hard winters and want of food from 939 to 942 (en.wikipedia.org 'Eldgja', read 7 Oct 2026; Oppenheimer and others 2018 (?))

seen.window: A hairy star before dawn.
seen.log: A star with hair, before dawn, for some weeks.

events.source: Halley's comet by reckoning and the Chinese record (?). For the north there is only William of Malmesbury's old monk Eilmer, who 'may have seen it in 989 and 1066' (Gesta regum II.225, about 1125: LATER). No northern annal of the year was found for it.

seen.window: The day goes dark over the fjord.
seen.log: The sun was darkened.

events.then: King Olaf fell at Stiklestad, by the Church's reckoning on 29 July 1030. His poet Sigvat says the sun went dark that day. Either the battle was on 31 August, or memory moved the darkness to the battle: the game does not say (?).
events.source: Sigvat Thordarson, Erfidrapa Olafs helga (about 1040); Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1030; the day of the eclipse by reckoning

events.date: seen in England from 1066-04-24, the eve of the Greater Litany, for seven nights

seen.window: The long-haired star, every night for a week.
seen.log: Such a sign was seen in the sky as no man had seen before. Some said it was the star called comet.

events.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (C, D) 1066; the Bayeux Tapestry ('these men wonder at the star'); it is Halley's

events.date: 799; no day or month is given

where.water: the strait and the southern North Sea
where.when: year = 799 and month >= 9 and month <= 10 and under_way

seen.window: The sea goes the colour of slate, then white. Other sails, then fewer.
seen.log: A great storm. Many ships were lost with their crews.

card.when: year = 799 and month >= 9 and month <= 10 and under_way
card.title: The year of the wrecks
card.intention: Three sails were in sight at noon. One is in sight now.

options.label: Run for the nearest beach and put her on it
Ride it out under bare pole, with a rope astern
Lighten her: the cargo goes over the side

events.then: The month is the game's (?): autumn, when the gales begin. The steersman's-child ghost and the empty ship lean on this year.
events.source: Historia regum 799: many ships were wrecked or sunk with their crews by a violent storm in the British sea

seen.window: The winter hard at night: thatch in the air, the tide over the bank and still coming.
seen.log: A great wind on the eve of the Lord's birth threw down houses, and the sea came over the land. Many cattle were drowned.

card.when: year = 800 and month = 12 and moored
card.title: Christmas Eve
card.intention: The boat is on the hard for the winter. The water is at her keel, and it is not yet the top of the tide.

options.label: Buy every hand in the ale-house and haul her higher
Double the ropes and trust them
Go to the vigil, or to the Yule board, and leave her to God or luck

events.then: The next morning, far to the south, the king is crowned emperor. The news takes six weeks to come.
events.source: Historia regum 800: a great wind on 24 December threw down towns and houses, the sea broke over its bounds, and many cattle died

where.water: any, at night, as a storm passes
where.when: under_way and storm >= 1 and (hour >= 21 or hour <= 4)

seen.window: A pale flame standing on the mast-head, and a second on the yard. It does not burn the wood.
seen.log: A light on the mast in the storm, that was not fire.

card.when: under_way and storm >= 1 and (hour >= 21 or hour <= 4)
card.title: The light on the mast
card.intention: It hisses a little. The men have stopped bailing to look at it.

options.label: Tell them the old saying: two lights are good, one alone is a wreck. There are two
Tell them to bail
Make a vow on it, aloud

events.then: Do not call it Saint Elmo's fire: the name is later (gods_cult.md, section 9). A vow made here is the chain storm_vow.
events.source: Pliny, Naturalis historia II.101: stars that settle on the yards of ships; two are a good sign, one alone sinks the ship (a book in every great library of the 790s)

where.water: any open water; likelier after a great storm
where.when: under_way and (flag.rare_799_rode or flag.rare_799_beached or flag.hr_donemuthe_witness or year >= 795)

seen.window: A hull lying beam-on to the swell, sail in rags, nobody at the helm.
seen.log: Met a ship with no one aboard.

card.when: under_way and not fog
card.title: Nobody aboard
card.intention: She is afloat and dry. There is a cooking pot on the hearth-stone with food in it.

options.label: Board her and see what she carries
Take her in tow to the nearest port and claim her before the reeve
Leave her. The crew will not thank you for anything else

events.then: What the sea throws up is the lord of the shore's: a towed ship is a law card in port (law_tolls.md, the section on wreck), unless the line hr_law_wreck was written in 802.
events.source: none needed: an ordinary thing after a gale (Historia regum 799). No tale is told about her; the game does not explain her.

where.water: off the dunes of Walichrum, in fog

seen.window: Nothing but grey. A bell, slow, somewhere to the south. Then from the north.
seen.log: A bell in the fog off the dunes.

card.when: under_way and fog >= 1
card.title: A bell
card.intention: One man says it is the church on the dune, rung for ships. One says there is no church on that side.

options.label: Steer for it, sounding as you go
Anchor and wait for the fog to lift

events.then: CHANGED from the fate page's 'drowned bell': a drowned church that rings is a seamen's tale of later centuries, and no source of the period has it. Here it is only a bell and two opinions. (The dunes of Walichrum did go under the sea, after the game's years.)
events.source: no period source (?); Design/content/dossiers/walichrum.md for the lost shore

where.water: in later lives, the far north-west
where.when: moored and (port.id = quentovic or port.id = dorestad or port.id = traiectum)

seen.window: In the first life, nothing: a tale told ashore.
seen.log: Heard of the navel of the sea, that swallows the water twice a day and throws it up again.

card.when: moored and (port.id = quentovic or port.id = dorestad or port.id = traiectum)
card.title: The navel of the sea
card.intention: A clerk who has been at court tells it as a thing written in a book: far to the north-west the sea has a throat.

options.label: Ask him where, exactly, and write it on the chart's edge
Tell him what a tide race is
Listen

events.source: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum I.6 (written about 790 by a man of Charles's court): the whirlpool that sucks in the waves and spews them out twice a day, and swallows ships; sea_lore.md section 5

where.water: north and west of the Faroes, in the lives when those waters are open

seen.window: A white line on the northern horizon that is not cloud; then floes, with a seal on one.
seen.log: Ice from the north, in June.

card.when: under_way and month >= 5 and month <= 7 and ice >= 1
card.title: Ice in June
card.intention: The air has gone cold in a breath. The lookout says the sea ahead has stopped moving.

options.label: Turn south at once
Run along its edge and see how far it goes

events.then: Not in the first life: the North Sea of 793 to 805 has no summer ice. For those years the frost of July 800 stands in its place.
events.source: Dicuil VII.13 (a day's sail north of Thule the sea was frozen); the Exeter Book's riddle of the iceberg (texts_793.json exeter_33_iceberg)

seen.window: If Colonia is open: a grey beast as high as a hay barn at the water's edge, drinking, with a crowd keeping its distance. In the first release: nothing, only talk.
seen.log: They say a beast called an elephant has come to the emperor from the king of the Persians.

card.when: year = 802 and month >= 6 and month <= 8 and moored and port.realm = franks
card.title: The beast from Baghdad
card.intention: A Rhine skipper is telling it for the price of a cup: ears like sails, a nose like an arm, and it kneels when the Jew who leads it speaks.

options.label: Buy him the cup and ask everything
Say you will believe it when you see it
Tell them the old books know the beast, and what its teeth are worth

events.then: See hours_793.json elephant_802. Its road north of the Alps is not recorded (?). It died in 810 at Lippeham on the Rhine: a later life can see that.
events.source: ARF 801, 802, 810; Dicuil VII (people of the Frankish realm saw the elephant in emperor Charles's time)

where.when: moored and year >= 900 and port.faith = old_gods

seen.window: A white bear on a chain on the foredeck of a small ship, and a thin man feeding it his own dinner.
seen.log: A white bear from the far north, going to a king.

card.when: moored and year >= 1047 and year <= 1064
card.title: The bear
card.intention: He has spent everything he owns on it and means to give it to the king of the Danes. The king of Norway's land lies between, and the king of Norway wants it.

options.label: Give him passage south
Offer to buy the bear
Give him a meal and send him on

events.then: He will not sell. The hour bear_1055 in hours_793.json is the same man.
events.source: Audunar thattr vestfirzka (13th century, of about 1050 to 1064): LATER. Landnamabok has a settler give king Harald a white bear and two cubs about 900: LATER. Not in the first life: no ship of 793 comes from where white bears are.

seen.window: A twisted white horn as long as a man, in a linen wrap, shown under a cloak.
seen.log: Shown the horn of a unicorn. It smells of fish.

card.when: moored and year >= 990
card.title: The horn
card.intention: The seller says it is the horn of the beast in the psalms, proof against every poison. A Greenland man aboard says he has eaten the fish it grows on.

options.label: Buy it, and sell it as what he says it is
Buy it, and sell it as a sea-beast's tooth
Leave it

events.then: The false name is worth five times the true one to an abbot or a king, and is a tale against the house if it is ever known.
events.source: No source of the period has the trade (?): walrus tooth is the ivory of the Viking Age (Ohthere, about 890); the long horn sold as the unicorn's is known from the 12th century on. Shown only after Greenland is settled (985 or 986).

where.when: moored and (port.id = witla or port.id = walichrum or port.id = sarre or port.id = medemelacha)

seen.window: A black hill on the sand at low water, with gulls on it and every soul of the place running.
seen.log: A whale came ashore on the ebb.

card.when: moored and (port.id = witla or port.id = walichrum or port.id = sarre or port.id = medemelacha)
card.title: The king of fish on the shingle
card.intention: Oil, meat, bone and hide for a village for a year. The lord of the shore will hear of it by evening.

options.label: Put the crew to cutting before anyone comes
Send to the reeve yourself, and ask the finder's share
Buy what the village cuts and salt it down: in Lent it is fish

events.then: No written law of 793 says whose a stranded whale is: by custom what the sea throws up is the lord of the shore's (the king's right to 'great fish' is written down centuries later).
events.source: The Franks Casket (Northumbria, about 700), made of the bone of a whale that 'grew sad where he swam onto the shingle'; Bede, Historia ecclesiastica I.1 (whales and seals taken on these coasts); saints_calendar.md section 4 (whale counts as fish in a fast); sea_lore.md on wreck

where.when: moored and port.id = ripa and month >= 6 and month <= 8

seen.window: A hooded bird on a block, nearly white, larger than any hawk you know.
seen.log: A white falcon from the north, in the summer market.

card.when: moored and port.id = ripa and month >= 6 and month <= 8
card.title: The white falcon
card.intention: The man who has it will not name a price to someone who cannot say which king it is for.

options.label: Name the king, and buy it for a gift
Ask how it is fed and carried at sea
Walk on

events.then: Given to a king or an archbishop, before witnesses, it is the best gift in the first life: a pip of Name and a great man's ear. It must be kept alive on the crossing.
events.source: Boniface, letter 105 (king Aethelberht II of Kent asks him, about 750, for two falcons that will take cranes, 'for few hawks of that kind are found in Kent') and letter 69 (he sends the king of the Mercians a hawk and two falcons). That the great white falcons of the far north came through Ripa in the 790s is a guess (?).

where.when: year = 796 and month >= 4 and month <= 7 and moored and (port.id = quentovic or port.id = lundenwic)

seen.window: A chest open on the toll house table: a belt with gold plates, a curved sword in a strange scabbard, two bolts of silk the colour of wine.
seen.log: Saw the gifts for the English king: a sword of the Huns, a belt, and silk.

card.when: year = 796 and month >= 4 and month <= 7 and moored and port.id = quentovic
card.title: The sword of the Huns
card.intention: The clerk is listing each piece before it crosses. It came out of the ring of the Avars, with fifteen wagon-loads more.

options.label: Ask to see how the blade is made
Tell the clerk what silk of that width fetches, so he writes it right
It is not yours to look at

events.source: Alcuin, letter 100 (Charles sends Offa a belt, a Hunnish sword and two silk cloaks); Historia regum 795 (the Avar treasure: fifteen wagons, each drawn by four oxen); ARF 796

seen.window: By word: a clock of brass, turned by water, that drops a little ball on a cymbal at each hour, and at the twelfth sends twelve horsemen out of twelve windows.
seen.log: Heard of the caliph's clock at the emperor's hall.

card.when: year = 807 and moored and port.realm = franks
card.title: The clock that counts by itself
card.intention: A man who has been to the palace says it rang the hours all night with nobody near it.

options.label: Ask how water can count
Ask whether such a thing would keep time at sea
The tide tells you the hour

events.source: ARF 807: the envoy of the king of the Persians, with two monks from the patriarch of Jerusalem, brought a tent, silks, perfumes, two brass candlesticks and a brass clock driven by water

seen.window: By word: a chest of pipes that sings when bellows are trodden.
seen.log: Heard that a priest is building the emperor an instrument that sings with wind.

card.when: year = 826 and moored and port.realm = franks
card.title: The pipes
card.intention: The palace is buying lead, tin and whole ox-hides for bellows, and paying well.

options.label: Bring the lead and tin he needs
Ask what it sounds like

events.correction: The fate page has 'an organ built for the emperor by a Greek'. The builder was George, a priest from Venice, who came to the emperor Louis in 826 saying he could make one and was sent to Aachen to do it. The organ a Greek emperor sent came to king Pippin in 757.
events.source: ARF 826; ARF 757

seen.window: On a shelf in a caster's booth, among moulds: a small bronze man sitting cross-legged on a flower, with a mark between his eyes.
seen.log: A little bronze god at Helgo. Nobody there knows whose.

card.when: moored and port.id = helgo
card.title: The bronze man
card.intention: The caster had it from his father, who had it from a man from the east. He keeps it because it is well made.

options.label: Ask every stranger in the place what it is
Offer silver for it
Leave it on its shelf

events.then: Nobody can tell you, in this life or any other in the game. He will not sell. Outside the twelve ports: for the release that opens the lake.
events.source: The Helgo Buddha: a bronze figure of the 6th century from the north of India, found on Helgo in the 1950s with a bishop's crozier head from Ireland and a ladle from Egypt; dossier helgo.md. The cards baltic_east_793.json already carry 'the bronze man'.

where.water: a sandbank island or the outer dunes near them

seen.window: A hut of driftwood and turf on a bar that covers at spring tides, and a thread of smoke.
seen.log: A man living alone on the outer bank. He did not speak.

card.when: under_way and month >= 5 and month <= 9
card.title: The man on the bank
card.intention: He comes down to the water's edge and stands. He does not wave, and he does not speak when you hail him.

options.label: Put bread and a skin of water on the sand, and go
Anchor and sit a tide with him in silence
Ask him to bless the boat
options.check: me.faith = christian or me.faith = christian_irish or me.faith = prime_signed

events.then: The fate page's 'nine years without speaking' is the game's. Whether he blesses you is shown by one movement of his hand, not said.
events.source: Dicuil VII.15 (hermits from Ireland lived on the northern islands for near a hundred years, and are gone now because of the Northmen); Bede, Vita Cuthberti c. 17-19 (the hermit of Farne); Alcuin's poem on the saints of York for the anchorites Balthere and Echa. A hermit on these particular banks is the game's (?).

seen.window: An old woman with an iron staff, seated apart at the edge of the market. People go to her one at a time and do not stay long.
seen.log: A woman at Ripa who sees for a price.

card.when: moored and port.id = ripa and month >= 5 and month <= 9
card.title: The woman with the staff
card.intention: She looks at your hands, not your face, and names a price before you have asked anything.

options.label: Pay, and hear what she says
Walk past
Tell the priest at home what goes on here

pay.troth: -1 if me.faith = christian; +1 if me.faith = old_gods

events.then: She says one plain sentence about the season ahead, drawn from a short list. The game never says whether it was true, and it never comes true in detail (gods_cult.md, section 5: must not).
events.source: Iron staffs in women's graves at Birka, Oseberg (834) and Fyrkat (finds); gods_cult.md 3.5. The seeress with a staff, cat-skin gloves and a hood lined with white cat-skin is Eiriks saga rauda c. 4 (13th century, of Greenland about 1000): LATER, and not to be copied into 793.

seen.window: A thin man in a herdsman's cloak at a fire in the reeds, who asks sharper questions than a herdsman would.
seen.log: A stranger in the marsh asked how many ships the Danes have in the Severn.

card.when: year = 878 and month >= 1 and month <= 3
card.title: The man by the fire
card.intention: He has good boots under the mud, and the men with him do not sit until he does.

options.label: Answer what he asks, and ask nothing
Call him what he is
Sell him bread at the marsh price

events.then: CHANGED from the fate page's 'a king in disguise in his own hall'. The harper-king in the enemy's camp is William of Malmesbury's, about 1125; the burned loaves are a saint's Life of about 1000. What the Chronicle gives is a king hiding in the fens with a small band for eleven weeks: the game shows that, and lets the player guess.
events.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 878; Asser c. 53; William of Malmesbury, Gesta regum II.121: LATER

where.when: moored and me.name >= 2 and (port.id = doccinga or port.id = lundenwic or port.id = medemelacha)

seen.window: A blind man by the fire with a small harp across his knees, and a boy to lead him.
seen.log: A singer put our name in his song.

card.when: moored and me.name >= 2 and (port.id = doccinga or port.id = lundenwic or port.id = medemelacha)
card.title: The singer knows your name
card.intention: He sings of old kings and their wars. Tonight, between two of them, he has a line about a ship. He is waiting to hear what it is worth.

options.label: Pay him well, before the whole house
Pay him the price of a cup
Pay him in kind: tell him something worth a song
options.check: flag.hr_donemuthe_witness or flag.hr_king_witness or flag.hr_boys_nudge or me.lore >= 3

events.then: A good verse travels: a pip of Name. A bad one travels faster: flag rare_verse_bad costs a pip in every Frisian or English port until a deed answers it. CHANGED from the fate page's 'skald': skalds are of the Norse courts of the next century. For 793 the singer is real: Bernlef (cast.bernlef), the blind Frisian who sang the deeds of the old kings, and the English scop.
events.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.25 (Bernlef, 'who knew well how to sing the deeds of the ancients and the wars of kings'); Widsith and Deor (texts_793.json deor)

where.when: year = 798 and moored and port.id = lundenwic

seen.window: From the river at night: the whole north bank lit from underneath, and the hard black with people.
seen.log: Lundenwic burned, and a great many people with it.

card.when: year = 798 and month >= 7 and month <= 9 and moored and port.id = lundenwic
card.title: The wic is burning
card.intention: It began up the north road and the wind is bringing it down to the shore. There is time to do one thing.

options.label: Get your own boat off the hard
Carry out the moneyer's irons and the reeve's chest
Take people off the hard, as many as she will float

events.then: The month is the game's (?): a dry one. See the pillar 798-london-fire-798. In 801 it burns again, soon after its bishop dies.
events.source: Historia regum 798, 801

seen.log: A man I never saw before knew whose boat this was.

card.when: moored and me.name >= 3 and port.visits <= 1
card.title: Your name, in a stranger's mouth
card.intention: You have never landed here. The man taking your rope says your name, and your house's, and something you did.

options.label: Say: that is so
Ask him what else is said
Say he has the wrong boat

events.then: It comes once, in the first port never visited after Name reaches three. What he says you did is the first deed in the save that was worth two points or more to his people.
events.source: Design/fate_faith_and_self.md section 5; reputation_793.json (news of a deed travels with the ships)

seen.log: Grey in the comb this winter.

card.when: moored and month = 12 and year >= 800
card.title: The first grey
card.intention: The portrait is a year older each winter. This is the winter it shows.

options.label: Laugh, and say the sea did it
Send for the one who will have the boat after you
Say nothing, and comb it under

events.then: The year is a guess for a merchant who began at about thirty: set it from the player's own age when the portrait knows it. Sending for the heir opens the chain house_heir early.
events.source: Design/DECISIONS.md, 7 October, ruling 3 (the portrait a year older each winter); Design/fate_faith_and_self.md section 5

also_in_other_files: Each past's ghost (three dated beats) is in self_793.json. The Avar wagons, the black stones and the elephant's road are in hours_793.json.
sources: NASA Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses and of Lunar Eclipses (Espenak and Meeus), tables 0701-0800 and 0801-0900, read 7 Oct 2026
